narrative:
Your application was denied because the model predicts a 60% chance you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt—a substantial risk for any law school. This prediction was not based on your gender or race, which were excluded from consideration. Instead, the strongest signals came from your academic performance during your own law studies, not from your family background or LSAT score alone.

The single most influential factor was your class standing in your third year. You placed in the 1st decile, meaning you were among the lowest-performing students in your cohort. Most accepted students fall near the 6th decile, so this gap is stark. Your first-year class standing also mattered, placing you in the 2nd decile against an accepted-student average around 6th decile. Together, these two rankings show a consistent pattern of struggling in law school coursework, which is a strong warning sign for bar exam readiness.

Interestingly, your undergraduate GPA worked in your favor. At 2.50, it is below the accepted average of 3.23, yet the model still treated it as a factor pushing toward passing, likely because other students with similar early law school performance had even lower GPAs. But this positive influence was not strong enough to offset the very concerning downward class ranks.

To improve your chances, focus on rebuilding your academic foundation. Retake challenging courses, seek academic support, and consider a bar preparation course before reapplying. Demonstrating that you can succeed in rigorous legal study will directly address the factors that drove this decision.
